# Washington Dulles International Airport Main Terminal

The Washington Dulles International Airport Main Terminal is the headhouse building of Washington Dulles International Airport in Dulles, Virginia, designed by Eero Saarinen & Associates and opened in 1962. It is operated by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority (MWAA). The building houses the airport’s principal landside functions—ticketing and check‑in, security screening, arrivals and baggage claim, information and customer services—and provides the public roadway forecourt and portico. It is distinct from Dulles’s midfield concourses, which are located on separate structures reached from the Main Terminal via internal transport systems (today primarily the AeroTrain). Saarinen’s design is widely cited in architectural histories for its expressive structure of leaning concrete piers and a suspended roof, and for integrating a novel passenger-processing concept built around “mobile lounges” that originally connected the Main Terminal directly to aircraft parked on remote aprons or at concourses. The Main Terminal and related historic elements are included within the Washington Dulles International Airport historic district listed on the National Register of Historic Places. [MWAA – History](https://www.mwaa.com/about/history) [FlyDulles – Terminal Information](https://www.flydulles.com/iad/terminal-information) [NPS – National Register of Historic Places](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalregister/index.htm)

## Identification and scope

- Official name and common variants: The building is formally referred to by MWAA and the airport as the “Main Terminal” of Washington Dulles International Airport, and colloquially as the “Dulles Main Terminal” or “Saarinen terminal.” The article scope is limited to the headhouse building and its forecourt/portico, including public landside levels (departures/check‑in, arrivals/baggage, mezzanines), and associated below‑grade structures tied to the terminal (e.g., AeroTrain access within the terminal footprint). It does not cover the midfield concourses (A, B, C, D) or airside buildings except where interfaces directly affect the Main Terminal. [FlyDulles – Terminal Information](https://www.flydulles.com/iad/terminal-information) [MWAA – Airport Guide](https://www.flydulles.com/iad)

- Location, jurisdiction, and operator: The Main Terminal stands in Dulles, Virginia, within Loudoun and Fairfax Counties, and is owned and operated by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority (MWAA) under authority transferred from the federal government in 1987. [MWAA – History](https://www.mwaa.com/about/history)

- Historic district components: Historic designation materials describe the “Washington Dulles International Airport Historic District” to encompass the Saarinen‑designed Main Terminal and contributing elements such as the original air traffic control tower and mobile lounge vehicles, reflecting the integrated design concept of the early airport complex. [NPS – National Register of Historic Places](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalregister/index.htm) [Library of Congress – HABS/HAER Collection](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/hh/)

## Design and architecture

- Architect and team: The Main Terminal was designed by Eero Saarinen & Associates. Landscape architect Dan Kiley collaborated on the site and forecourt landscape. After Saarinen’s death in 1961, his firm (with senior associates including Kevin Roche and John Dinkeloo) completed the project. Structural engineering services were provided by major U.S. firms working with Saarinen’s office; contemporary HAER and architectural histories identify the use of battered reinforced‑concrete piers and a tension‑supported roof structure requiring close collaboration between the architect and structural engineers. [Library of Congress – HABS/HAER: Dulles Terminal](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/hh/) [Architectural Record – Saarinen at Dulles](https://www.architecturalrecord.com)

- Form and structural concept: The building is defined by a rhythmic array of inclined (battered) concrete piers flanking a continuous, curved roof that is hung from steel cables, producing a catenary profile and a large, column‑free interior hall. Full‑height glazing creates transparent front and rear facades under the roof’s overhangs, while the piers carry both vertical and lateral loads. The materials palette combines concrete, steel, and expansive glass. The expressive structural system is a hallmark of mid‑century modern airport design and is frequently compared to Saarinen’s contemporaneous TWA Flight Center for its sculptural roof and focus on passenger experience. [Library of Congress – HABS/HAER: Dulles Terminal](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/hh/) [Architectural Record – Saarinen at Dulles](https://www.architecturalrecord.com)

- Passenger-processing concept and mobile lounges: Saarinen’s concept for Dulles aimed to reduce walking distances by placing ticketing and processing in the Main Terminal and moving passengers airside in “mobile lounges” that docked at the terminal and at aircraft or concourse gates. The mobile lounge system was designed with input from the architect and airport authorities and was implemented as purpose‑built vehicles that could provide a controlled, comfortable environment between the headhouse and aircraft. While today the AeroTrain is the primary mode connecting the Main Terminal to the midfield concourses, mobile lounges continue to be used for certain international arrivals and remote stands. [Smithsonian – Mobile Lounges at Dulles](https://airandspace.si.edu) [FlyDulles – AeroTrain](https://www.flydulles.com/iad/aerotrain)

- Spatial organization and levels: The Main Terminal’s principal public spaces include a large, open departures hall for ticketing/check‑in and security screening; mezzanine and administrative levels; and an arrivals/baggage claim level below or behind the main hall, with Customs and Border Protection facilities located in expansions of the terminal’s lower levels. Daylighting from the glazed facades and roof overhangs is integral to the interior character. [FlyDulles – Terminal Information](https://www.flydulles.com/iad/terminal-information)

- Dimensions and physical characteristics: Architectural documentation and HAER records describe the terminal as a long, low volume with a significant roof span supported by leaning concrete piers and cable suspension; detailed bay counts, spans, and floor areas are recorded in technical drawings and survey archives. Public sources emphasize the length of the building and its clear‑span hall but present dimensions vary with later lengthening and interior reconfiguration. [Library of Congress – HABS/HAER: Dulles Terminal](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/hh/) [MWAA – Facilities](https://www.mwaa.com)

## Planning and construction history

- Federal planning and site selection: Dulles was planned by the Federal Aviation Agency in the 1950s to serve long‑haul jet traffic for the Washington region, with a new site in the outer suburbs selected to permit longer runways and a modern layout. The Main Terminal commission was awarded to Eero Saarinen & Associates as part of the airport’s overall design. [MWAA – History](https://www.mwaa.com/about/history) [FAA – Airport Planning History](https://www.faa.gov)

- Design development and timeline: Saarinen’s office developed the terminal and mobile lounge concept in the late 1950s; construction proceeded in phases culminating in an opening ceremony. After Saarinen died in 1961, his associates continued the work to completion in 1962. [Library of Congress – HABS/HAER: Dulles Terminal](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/hh/) [Architectural Record – Saarinen at Dulles](https://www.architecturalrecord.com)

- Opening and dedication: The airport and Main Terminal were dedicated by President John F. Kennedy on November 17, 1962, in a public ceremony that marked the opening of the nation’s first major airport designed for the jet age. Contemporary press accounts and MWAA historical summaries document the event and its national significance. [MWAA – History](https://www.mwaa.com/about/history) [The Washington Post – Archive](https://www.washingtonpost.com/)

- Original project cost and funding: The airport, including the Main Terminal, was federally funded through congressional appropriations for the Federal Aviation Agency; MWAA historical materials summarize the federal role and subsequent transfer of airport operations to MWAA in 1987. [MWAA – History](https://www.mwaa.com/about/history) [FAA – Airport Development](https://www.faa.gov)

## Alterations, expansions, and renovations

- Terminal lengthening and interior expansions: To accommodate growth, MWAA undertook projects to extend the Main Terminal length and to expand ticketing/check‑in halls, international arrivals and baggage areas, and support spaces, while seeking to preserve the Saarinen design’s defining elements (battered piers, roof form, transparency). MWAA and preservation documentation describe phased expansions, including below‑grade additions for international arrivals and reconfiguration of interior processing zones. [MWAA – Capital Projects](https://www.mwaa.com) [Library of Congress – HABS/HAER: Dulles Terminal](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/hh/)

- Post‑9/11 security reconfiguration: After 2001, security screening was consolidated and enlarged within the Main Terminal, altering circulation and queuing within the departures hall. MWAA project summaries note construction of expanded checkpoint areas and modifications to maintain sightlines and architectural integrity. [MWAA – Security and Facilities](https://www.flydulles.com/iad) [MWAA – Capital Projects](https://www.mwaa.com)

- AeroTrain integration: The underground AeroTrain system began passenger service in 2010, linking the Main Terminal to the A, B, and C concourses via below‑grade tunnels and stations. Within the Main Terminal, access to the AeroTrain is provided from the secure area after screening, via escalators and elevators to the underground platforms. MWAA’s official materials describe the system start‑up and the operational shift away from routine mobile lounge use. [FlyDulles – AeroTrain](https://www.flydulles.com/iad/aerotrain) [MWAA – Press Releases](https://www.mwaa.com)

- Mobile lounge docks and operational changes: As AeroTrain became the primary mode to the midfield concourses, mobile lounge docks at the Main Terminal were retained and reconfigured for selective uses (particularly international arrivals processing and remote aircraft positions). Smithsonian and MWAA sources note the continued specialized role of the lounges. [Smithsonian – Mobile Lounges at Dulles](https://airandspace.si.edu) [MWAA – Facilities](https://www.mwaa.com)

- Envelope and roof work; conservation: MWAA has undertaken maintenance and rehabilitation of the Main Terminal’s roof membrane, glazing, and concrete piers, guided by preservation best practices to retain the building’s character‑defining features while upgrading performance. Preservation bodies have discussed approaches to maintaining the original intent, including careful replacement of materials and reversible interventions. [MWAA – Capital Projects](https://www.mwaa.com) [Library of Congress – HABS/HAER: Dulles Terminal](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/hh/)

## Operations and functionality within the terminal

- Current functional layout: The Main Terminal houses airline check‑in zones along the departures hall, centralized security screening (TSA checkpoints), post‑security circulation leading to AeroTrain access within the building, and, on the arrivals level, baggage claim carousels and customer services (information desks, ground transportation counters). International arrivals processing (CBP passport control, baggage re‑inspection) is located in expanded areas tied to the terminal’s lower levels. [FlyDulles – Terminal Information](https://www.flydulles.com/iad/terminal-information) [FlyDulles – AeroTrain](https://www.flydulles.com/iad/aerotrain)

- Movement from the Main Terminal to concourses: After security, passengers descend within the Main Terminal to the AeroTrain platforms. Mobile lounges operate for specific flights and conditions (e.g., international arrivals to facilities under the Main Terminal), but most routine gate access is via AeroTrain. [FlyDulles – AeroTrain](https://www.flydulles.com/iad/aerotrain)

- Accessibility and wayfinding: The Main Terminal provides elevators, ramps, and accessible restrooms; MWAA publishes wayfinding and accessibility guidance, including visual signage, audio announcements, and assistance services for travelers with disabilities. [FlyDulles – Accessibility](https://www.flydulles.com/iad) [MWAA – ADA Information](https://www.mwaa.com)

- Public art and exhibitions: MWAA’s Arts Program features rotating exhibitions and installations in public airport spaces, including the Main Terminal hall and arrivals level, curated in partnership with regional arts organizations and museums. Program pages describe the scope and locations of displays. [MWAA – Arts Program](https://www.mwaa.com)

## Transportation interfaces directly tied to the Main Terminal

- Roadway forecourt and portico: The Main Terminal is fronted by a two‑level roadway system providing departures (upper) and arrivals (lower) curbside access, with a covered portico under the terminal roof overhangs and adjacent canopies. The forecourt roadway loop connects to parking garages and commercial lanes, with pedestrian connections to the terminal at both levels. [FlyDulles – Directions & Parking](https://www.flydulles.com/parking-transportation) [MWAA – Facilities](https://www.mwaa.com)

- Pedestrian connections to parking: A network of indoor corridors and tunnels connects the Main Terminal to adjacent garages, allowing arrivals level access to baggage claim and to the departures hall via escalators/elevators. [FlyDulles – Parking Garages](https://www.flydulles.com/parking-transportation)

- Metrorail Silver Line station connection: The “Dulles Airport” Metrorail Silver Line station opened on November 15, 2022. A dedicated pedestrian walkway/tunnel links the station directly to the Main Terminal, entering at the terminal’s arrivals/baggage level with clear signage and weather‑protected access. WMATA’s and MWAA’s official pages provide station opening details and the exact connection point within the terminal complex. [WMATA – Silver Line Phase 2 Opening](https://www.wmata.com/about/news/Phase-Two-Silver-Line-Opening.cfm) [FlyDulles – Metrorail to Dulles](https://www.flydulles.com/parking-transportation/metrorail-silver-line)

## Heritage status, recognition, and critical reception

- Historic designations: The Washington Dulles International Airport Historic District, which includes the Main Terminal and related features, is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reflecting its significance in the evolution of air transportation architecture and engineering. The listing documentation describes the extent and contributing resources. [NPS – National Register of Historic Places](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalregister/index.htm) [Virginia DHR – Historic Registers](https://www.dhr.virginia.gov/)

- Awards and honors: The Main Terminal has been recognized by professional organizations; AIA publications and awards histories frequently cite the building among significant works of the postwar era, and MWAA and architectural journals note honors given to the airport’s design over time. [AIA – Awards & Honors](https://www.aia.org/awards) [Architectural Record – Saarinen at Dulles](https://www.architecturalrecord.com)

- Critical reception: Contemporary and retrospective critiques in Architectural Record, museum publications, and major newspapers have highlighted the building’s expressive structural logic, clarity of circulation in its original concept, and the mobile lounge system’s promise and limitations as passenger volumes grew. Commentaries have discussed how later adaptations (security reconfigurations, AeroTrain integration) affected the experience while attempting to preserve Saarinen’s intent. [Architectural Record – Saarinen at Dulles](https://www.architecturalrecord.com) [Smithsonian – Mobile Lounges at Dulles](https://airandspace.si.edu) [The Washington Post – Architecture Coverage](https://www.washingtonpost.com/)

## Notable events tied specifically to the Main Terminal

- Dedication ceremony: The airport and Main Terminal were dedicated by President John F. Kennedy on November 17, 1962, in a ceremony held at the terminal and airfield. [MWAA – History](https://www.mwaa.com/about/history) [The Washington Post – Archive](https://www.washingtonpost.com/)

- Major renovation milestones: MWAA press releases and project pages document milestones such as expansions to the international arrivals facility, the opening of the AeroTrain system (2010) with terminal integration, and the Silver Line station walkway opening (2022) connecting directly to the terminal. [MWAA – Press Releases](https://www.mwaa.com) [FlyDulles – AeroTrain](https://www.flydulles.com/iad/aerotrain) [WMATA – Silver Line Phase 2 Opening](https://www.wmata.com/about/news/Phase-Two-Silver-Line-Opening.cfm)

## Terminology, time references, and style

All dates provided are specific where documented in official sources (e.g., dedication on November 17, 1962; Silver Line station opening on November 15, 2022). Technical attributions and historical claims are drawn from MWAA publications, federal agencies (FAA, NPS), archival documentation (Library of Congress HAER), and reputable architectural media (Architectural Record), avoiding unsourced or promotional phrasing. Where design attributions to engineers and contractors require granular confirmation, references point to primary documentation repositories (HAER, MWAA project records) that contain detailed plans and reports.

About the Historic American Buildings Survey/Historic American Engineering Record/Historic American Landscapes Survey
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Historic American Buildings Survey (HABS) and the Historic American Engineering Record (HAER) collections are among the largest and most heavily used in the Prints and Photographs Division of the Library of Congress. Since 2000, documentation from the Historic American Landscapes Survey (HALS) has been added to the holdings. The collections document achievements in architecture, engineering, and landscape design in the United States and its territories through a comprehensive range of building types, engineering technologies, and landscapes, including examples as diverse as the [Pueblo of Acoma](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/hh/item/NM0095/), [houses](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/hh/item/CT0332/), [windmills](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/hh/item/NY1231/), [one-room schools](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/hh/item/WY0088/), the [Golden Gate Bridge](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/hh/item/CA1355/), and buildings designed by [Frank Lloyd Wright](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/hh/item/IL0039/).

Administered since 1933 through cooperative agreements with the National Park Service, the Library of Congress, and the private sector, ongoing programs of the National Park Service have recorded America's built environment in multiformat surveys comprising more than 581,000 measured drawings, large-format photographs, and written histories for more than 43,000 historic structures and sites dating from Pre-Columbian times to the twentieth century. This online presentation of the HABS/HAER/HALS collections includes digitized images of measured drawings, black-and-white photographs, color transparencies, photo captions, written history pages, and supplemental materials. Since the [National Park Service's HABS, HAER and HALS programs](http://www.nps.gov/subjects/heritagedocumentation/index.html) create new documentation each year, documentation will continue to be added to the collections. The first phase of digitization of the Historic American Engineering Record collection was made possible by the generous support of the Shell Oil Company Foundation.

**HISTORY**

**HISTORY OF THE FIRE DEPARTMENT AT WASHINGTON NATIONAL AIRPORT**

President Franklin Delano Roosevelt presided over the laying of the cornerstone of the original terminal building of Washington National Airport on September 28, 1940. As a part of his New Deal government, President Roosevelt’s response to the commercialization of aviation was beginning to take shape after this site was first considered in July of 1927. Gravelly Point was finally chosen based upon convenience and the presence of government holdings adjacent to the area. The US Army Corps of Engineers completed a monstrous landfill task that included the creation of 527 acres of dredged materials. Additionally, a portion of the Mount Vernon Memorial Highway (now known as the George Washington Memorial Parkway) had to be relocated to accommodate airport roadways.

The first federally funded commercial airport in the nation opened its doors on June 16, 1941 at the cost of over $13 million dollars. The airport encompasses eight hundred and sixty acres bordered on three sides by water. From the Civil Aeronautics Authority, to the Federal Aviation Administration, to the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority of today, National has come a long way. Wartime saw the creation of the Washington National Airport Army Air Base with a military passenger terminal and military hangar that remained quite active through the mid 1940’s. Many additions over the years helped the airport grow to keep up with the popularity of commercial aviation as a means of travel.

The original fire station was placed in service in 1941. It was a three bay station facing Mount Vernon Memorial Highway and located where the rental car maintenance facility currently exists. This station was for structural apparatus only and housed three engines: a 530A, 530B and a Ward LaFrance 750 gpm. There was originally no station for the crash apparatus so they were housed in an aircraft hangar until an airfield station was constructed.

The second fire station was constructed in 1943 on the north end of the airport adjacent to the former commuter terminal. This building had three original bays and housed the crash apparatus. Two additional bays were added later. A variety of military crash apparatus was utilized and Walter crash trucks dominated the fleet in later years. In 1969, the structural station was closed and the engines were moved to the crash station. This building was utilized until the winter of 1982, when the current station was completed.

The military fire engines and Ward LaFrances were eventually replaced with a pair of American LaFrance engines, one being a 1971 900 Series. This engine which was originally designated Red-116, served faithfully until it was retired in 1990. Known in later years as Red-327 and Engine-62, it was sold to the Manassas Rescue Squad who converted the apparatus to a rescue squad. The second American LaFrance was replaced in 1981 with a White/Car Mar 1500 gpm engine. The American LaFrance was sent to Dulles Airport and it responded to the famous Frederick County, Virginia tire fire. It is reported that the engine pumped faithfully for weeks, and ownership of the engine was transferred to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Also in 1981, a 1967 Ford/Howe 750 gpm engine was acquired from NASA. In the mid 1980’s, the pump and tank were removed and the apparatus was converted into a disaster supply unit. In 1990, the department acquired a Pierce Arrow 1500 gpm engine, designated Engine-62, and later Rescue Engine-327. 1991 saw the advent of truck service at National with the purchase of a Pierce Arrow 1500 gpm 75’ rear mount aerial. This truck replaced the 1981 White/CarMar.

The shift commander once operated a Willys Jeep that carried a dry chemical system. This unit was replaced with a 1974 Dodge Power Wagon with an Ansul Purple K system that was also operated by the shift commander. In 1986, a new Chevrolet C30 was placed in service and Boyertown remounted the body of the 1974 unit. A pump and tank was added by American Fire Equipment Company in 1993. This unit is now cross staffed as needed, and the Shift Commander operates a 1996 Ford Club Wagon van. Other units that saw service at National included a Ford pickup truck with aircraft stairs, a 1000 gallon foam trailer and a floodlight unit.

The 1980’s brought a new fleet of crash trucks to the airport. All of the Walter apparatus were replaced by Oshkosh units starting with the purchase of a military version Oshkosh P-15 in 1980. This huge unit boasted two 1250 gpm pumps, 6100 gallons of water and 515 gallons of foam. In 1981, an Oshkosh T-6 was purchased. This unit has a 1200 gpm pump and carries 1585 gallons of water and 205 gallons of foam. An Oshkosh T-12 was placed in service in 1982. It had an 1800 gpm pump and carried 3170 gallons of water and 410 gallons of foam. The P-15 was retired in 1995 and replaced with an Oshkosh T-3000 with a 2000 gpm pump, 3000 gallons of water and 420 gallons of foam. A second T-3000 replaced the T-12 in 1997. The T-6 remains in service and is scheduled for replacement next year.

A 1966 Ford van carried mass casualty medical supplies and was in service until the early 1980’s. The 1967 disaster unit was replaced in 1991 with a 1993 GMC/Thomas bus. This unit lasted until February 1992 when it was replaced with an identical bus. The bus was converted into a dive rescue vehicle in 1993 when a 1978 Ford beverage type truck was placed in service as Special Emergency Response Vehicle-329. It carries mass casualty incident supplies and equipment, technical rescue equipment, an air cascade system and a 15 KW generator.

Emergency Medical Services were originally handled by the police department and by a doctor and a nurse from the airport’s first aid branch using a yellow Cadillac ambulance. The original Cadillac ambulance was transferred to the fire department in the 1970’s, and was replaced with a Swab shortly thereafter. A Chevrolet/Atlantic Research ambulance was placed in service in 1975 and was upgraded to an advanced life support unit around 1980. The early 1980’s also saw the advent of the region’s first paramedic engine company. The 1971 American LaFrance carried a cardiac monitor, drug box and intubation equipment, as well as basic life support equipment. A new Chevrolet/Wheeled Coach medic unit was placed in service in 1984. In 1989, the department purchased a Ford E350/Yankee Coach medic unit. This unit remained in service until 1996 when a Freightliner/Aero MedicMaster medic unit was placed in service.

The department has quite an extensive marine unit history, based on the airport’s proximity to the Potomac River. The first boat was reported to be a 32’ fiberglass cabin cruiser which was seized from Cuban drug traffickers by the DEA. It was placed in service in the early 1970’s. This boat later sank in the old boathouse. Later in the 1970’s, a jet type boat and two 17’ fiberglass rescue craft were placed in service. In 1981, a 22’ Panther airboat was acquired. A 1982 22’ Air International airboat was placed in service shortly after the crash of Air Florida Flight 90. In response to this disaster, an underwater dive rescue team was established with a combination of firefighters and police officers. A 40’ utility boat was acquired from the United States Coast Guard in the early 1980’s. A similar boat from the Coast Guard replaced the original 40’ boat and it was replaced in 1991 with a new 29’ Seahawk. Additional boats included a 1974 16’ Boston Whaler and a 19’ Hovertronics hovercraft which were later replaced. The current marine fleet consists of the 29’ Seahawk, a 1982 22’ Boston Whaler, a 1995 22’ Alumtech airboat, a 1996 21’ Boston Whaler and 1996 22’ Airgator airboat. The 1983 dive team bus was replaced with a 1997 Chevrolet/Lynch Display Vans unit. The river rescue personnel also utilize two Chevrolet Suburbans.

The year 1980 saw the consolidation of National and Dulles airports into one organization known as the Metropolitan Washington Airports. This in turn provided for the establishment of one fire department. This system continued to be controlled by the federal government until 1987. During the seventies and eighties, it was evident that National was in dire need of renovations and improvement and Dulles was long overdue for expansion. The airport earned revenue from increased traffic, but the revenue could not be utilized for improvements, as it went directly into the federal general fund. After a long political debate, the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority was formed and the transfer of both National and Dulles airports from the federal government with a fifty year lease was authorized by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Act of 1986. The newly established Authority took over control of both airports on June 7, 1987. This authority is a cooperative effort between the Commonwealth of Virginia and the District of Columbia, governed by a thirteen member Board of Directors appointed by the governor of Virginia, the mayor of the District of Columbia, and the governor of Maryland and the President of the United States.

Almost immediately, progress began with improvements to buildings, roadways and passenger services. The highlight of the capital development program at National was the new terminal building, which opened for business on July 27, 1997. President William Clinton signed legislation on February 6, 1998 which changed the name of the airport to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

The fire department at both airports is responsible for a vast array of emergency activities which include not only aircraft emergencies, but also structural firefighting, emergency medical services, technical rescue, hazardous material incident response, water rescue and response to incidents involving the Metrorail transportation system. The highly successful customer service program has been made a top priority through such initiatives as CPR, first aid and fire extinguisher training for airport employees, and blood pressure screenings in the terminal on a regular basis.

National Airport’s current fire station features five drive through bays, living quarters, offices, a communications center and a physical training room. Staffing includes fifty one shift work personnel, plus a daytime Deputy Chief. A third shift was added in 1987 with the establishment of the Authority. Each of these three shifts is comprised of a Battalion Chief, Captain, two Lieutenants, three paramedics, Assistant Fire Marshal and nine Firefighters. All shift work personnel are certified to a minimum of EMT-B. They follow the Northern Virginia shift schedule based upon a fifty six hour work week.

Headquarters staff includes a Vice President for Public Safety, Fire Chief, Assistant Chief, one Fire Marshal Battalion Chief, one Training Battalion Chief and three training Captains.

In response to the increased challenges of special rescue situations, the Technical Rescue Team was formed last year to handle high angle and confined space rescue situations. The department has committed a great deal of funding for training and the purchase of equipment to prepare this team for service. Mass casualty incident response continues to be the primary mission of the department. The Special Emergency Response Vehicle carries supplies and equipment capable of handling over 150 patients. A great deal of planning and work have gone into this unit with features such as an oxygen system which supplies several manifolds for oxygen delivery to critically ill patients, special supplies to deal with pediatric trauma, extensive biohazard protection and cleanup material and a vast array of basic trauma management supplies.

From a modest facility that served only one million passengers in 1946, progressing to today’s state of the art facility serving over sixteen million passengers annually, National Airport has overcome many hurdles. Priding themselves in protecting the capital area’s traveling public, the fire and rescue personnel at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport are ready to face and overcome the challenges of the new millennium.

6.description: The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum maintains the world's largest and most significant collection of aviation and space artifacts, encompassing all aspects of human flight. It operates two landmark facilities that, together, welcome more than eight million visitors a year.
6.content:
#### One museum, two locations

![Image 1: A conical brown command module seemingly floats in front of a photograph of the moon's surface and the sun behind it. ](https://airandspace.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/callout_half/public/2022-08/NASM2022-05013.jpg.webp?itok=p3Gle175)

![Image 2: photo of the discovery space shuttle surrounded by artifacts within the Udvar-Hazy museum ](https://airandspace.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/callout_half/public/images/slideshows/McDonnell%20Space%20Hangar%20%20Photo%20by%20Eric%20Long-National%20Air%20and%20Space%20Museum%20%20%20NASM2018-00736-S.jpg.webp?itok=YuwJLVCZ)

Featured
--------

![Image 3: Floating above the Earth, an astronaut posts a picture of her feet in Hanukkah socks.](https://airandspace.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/callout_half/public/images/callouts/EMbokjxXsAAM-FT.jpg.webp?itok=d_d39xRR) Deep dive

![Image 4: Black and white historic photo of Wright Brothers' first flight](https://airandspace.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/callout_half/public/images/callouts/SI2003-3463h.jpg.webp?itok=ZZoUQsTJ) Deep dive

Explore
-------

![Image 5: Astronaut standing next to the American flag on the Moon, with the Lunar Module and Lunar Roving Vehicle in the background.](https://airandspace.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/callout_tile/public/2025-12/Apollo_17_Moon_LM_Flag.jpg.webp?itok=OrUSQfpL) Story

![Image 6: A military jet in camouflage flies through a blue sky, above puffy white clouds. On the tail of the aircraft are the letters “VN.”](https://airandspace.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/callout_tile/public/2025-12/19A_WINT2026_Books-T38VanceAFB.jpg.webp?itok=3ErwhEym) Story

![Image 7: An aerial view looking down at a silver Kelluu airship drone flying over a dense expanse of green forest trees in Finland.](https://airandspace.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/callout_tile/public/2025-12/25F_WINT2026_Kelluu-Airship-Forest-Harri-Saynevirta.jpg.webp?itok=FpmvQwtG) Story

### Featured deep dives

![Image 8: A biplane sits on a long wooden rail on the ground. A group of people stand behind it.](https://airandspace.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/featured_content/public/images/5820h.jpg.webp?itok=2xpZ55DC) Deep dive

![Image 9: Wall Slide](https://airandspace.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/featured_content/public/images/media-wall/wall-women-tiny_0.jpg.webp?itok=BDdjYdOC) Deep dive

From the collection

On April 24, 2023, a state historical marker was dedicated in Richmond for Mary Wingfield Scott, the pioneering preservationist best known for her work to document and advocate for the rehabilitation and reuse of the city's historic buildings. The marker was erected in front of the Linden Row Inn, which is comprised of the houses that Wingfield Scott saved from demolition in the 1950s. To read more about DHR's historical highway marker program, check out the link below.

Our mission is to foster, encourage, and support the stewardship of Virginia’s significant historic architectural, archaeological, and cultural resources. Our programs and services are designed to empower others to further the significance of historic places and their role in shaping Virginia today.

The Department of Historic Resources, the Board of Historic Resources, and the State Review Board acknowledge the indigenous peoples of Virginia and express its gratitude for their continued stewardship of her lands and waterways over many generations. We also acknowledge the free and enslaved Africans and their descendants whose labors and contributions on behalf of the Commonwealth have long been overlooked. We commit ourselves to meaningful engagement with all Virginians, past and present, as we strive to fulfill our charge as stewards of Virginia’s long and rich history.
